title: Tabulating Truth: Why Karnaugh Maps Work
excerpt: The algebra behind Karnaugh maps: what a minterm is, why adjacency matters, and why relabeling a truth table with Gray code is the entire trick.

body.text: Tabulating Truth: Why Karnaugh Maps Work

content.text: A Karnaugh map (K-map) looks like a grid-drawing trick, but it isn't a new piece of math bolted onto Boolean algebra. It's a truth table with its rows and columns reordered so that one algebraic identity, applied over and over, becomes something you can spot with your eyes instead of derive with algebra.
Every combinational circuit can be written as a truth table: one row per input combination, one output column per output. A row where the output is 1 corresponds to a

, a product term that's true for exactly that one input combination. Sum every minterm together and you get the canonical Sum-of-Products (SOP) form of the function. It's guaranteed correct, and it's almost never the simplest circuit you could actually build.

body.text: The One Identity Behind Every Simplification

content.text: Simplification comes down to one algebraic identity, applied repeatedly: X + X' = 1. If two minterms are identical except for a single variable that appears true in one and complemented in the other, that variable cancels.

body.code:
AB'C + ABC
= AB(C' + C)
= AB * 1
= AB

content.text: That's the entire mechanism. Two minterms merge into one shorter term whenever they differ in exactly one bit position. A K-map doesn't add new math on top of this, it just makes it fast to spot which pairs, quads, or larger groups of minterms qualify, by eye instead of by hand-manipulating algebra.

body.text: The Problem With an Ordinary Truth Table

content.text: Write a truth table in ordinary binary counting order (000, 001, 010, 011, ...) and rows that differ by exactly one bit end up scattered across the table instead of sitting next to each other. Row 011 and row 100 look adjacent on paper, but they differ in all three bits, they're as far apart as two minterms can possibly be. Spotting mergeable pairs by eye in that ordering gets painful fast past two variables.
Instead of counting in ordinary binary, label the rows and columns in

: 00, 01, 11, 10. Every consecutive pair in that sequence differs in exactly one bit. Counting this way, separately, for rows and for columns of a grid is the single design decision that makes everything else about a Karnaugh map work.

body.code:
Binary counting order:  00  01  10  11   <- 01 and 10 differ in 2 bits, not adjacent-safe
Gray code order:        00  01  11  10   <- every neighbor differs in exactly 1 bit

body.text: What a Karnaugh Map Actually Is

content.text: A Karnaugh map is the same truth table you already know, poured into a grid whose rows and columns are labeled in Gray code instead of counting order. Because of that labeling, any two cells that touch, including the pair formed by the leftmost and rightmost column, or the top and bottom row wrapping around the edge, are guaranteed to represent minterms differing in exactly one variable.

Geometric adjacency on the page becomes a direct stand-in for "these two terms are legally mergeable." That's the whole trick, and it's why grouping cells by eye works at all, why K-maps aren't just a truth table redrawn for no reason.

The rest of this guide walks the same idea across three grid sizes: a 2-variable map to see the mechanics with nothing else in the way, a 3-variable map to see the wraparound rule in action for the first time, and a 4-variable map to see it happen along both axes at once, including the classic four-corners group.
